Undercity

On Mars, radiation is not weather — it is geography. The surface takes ~230 mSv a year; 30 m of rock takes that down to Earth background, for free, forever. So the city keeps its machines upstairs and its people below: a camouflaged gate in a berm, an elevator whose speed limit is set by your ears, a quarter with a hydroponic wall and one real tree, and a clinic. Five assets, every number on this page traceable to a ledger.

01

Two doors in a hill

The entrance had one hard constraint: the terrain engine cannot dig. So the undercity begins with an illusion — a 60 m artificial berm raised over flat ground, with a level roadway cut straight into its face.

The berm is fourteen overlapping regolith lobes, top-flattened, piled to 14.5 m — reading as a hill from every angle while hiding a horizontal portal. The portal itself is built in the city's printed-regolith language: 0.5 m print layers with alternating ridge depth, the same signature as the surface print works. At the end of a 12 m gallery, a 6 × 5 m sliding vehicle airlock with hazard-striped seam and an 8-lamp cycle indicator; beside it, a personnel airlock with a glowing porthole. At night the gallery's floor-level light strips make the doorway the only warm thing on the hill — the one-glance proof that someone is home.

Forty-two meters west stands the second door: hab-lift-01, the personnel elevator headframe. A print-layer blockhouse, a white hoist room with a service beam, and a stainless double door under red/green cycle lamps — 1444 triangles total. Vehicles take the gate; people take the shaft.

02

The ride down

The residential level sits under 30 m of rock; the main shafts continue to the −3000 m deep levels, where the dark-matter experiment lives. Four analytic accounts shaped the elevator — and the most interesting limit is not the motor.

Rope, 1/g. Hoist rope self-weight scales with gravity, so a 3000 m Martian shaft loads its rope like an 1140 m terrestrial one. On Earth this depth means staged hoists and transfer stations; on Mars a single friction-drive belt runs pit-to-portal, margin 2.4×.

Ears, 52 Pa/s. The shaft is pressurized, and 3000 m of gas column adds ~13 kPa of self-weight between portal and pit bottom. At the rated 12 m/s the pressure ramp is 52 Pa/s — comfortably inside the ~300 Pa/s ear-comfort envelope. The cab could go faster; your ears could not.

Power, 47 kW. Counterweighted, the drive only fights the 900 kg payload imbalance: 47 kW peak at low gravity, and each descent regenerates ~7 kWh back into the storage yard. Leakage, 7×10⁻⁷ sr. A straight shaft is a skylight for cosmic rays — but depth is its own collimator: the pit subtends a solid angle that makes the direct beam negligible, and a borated cab-roof plug seals the docking gap.

Below, the foyer is the interchange: a 20 × 12 m vaulted vehicle airlock hall (6 m³ personnel cycle: 0.2 kWh, 3 minutes, 90% gas recovery) with the elevator doors on its right wall — and, on its left, a viewport. Behind that window a 2500-triangle diorama fakes the whole cavern city: tower silhouettes, lit-window grids, street lamps, a skylight band. The cheapest square meters in the district buy its most important sentence: there is a city down here.

03

Living under rock

hab-quarter-01 is the residential block: five cabins, a hydroponic wall, a commons, one real tree — and three recliner pods that hold the city's strangest statistic.

Each cabin is 9.6 m² of private, acoustically padded space with its own air feed — and 30 m of rock overhead, which means residential radiation shielding needs no active hardware at all. The magenta wall is not decor: chlorophyll eats 430 and 660 nm, so the farm's LEDs emit exactly those bands — 29 m² of canopy at 2.8 µmol/J, a 4 kW wall yielding order-25 kg of greens a month. Its water loop closes at >90% vapor recovery; the ~17 L/day makeup is a few percent of the Rodwell well's Stefan-checked 669-sol ledger.

The commons runs 3000 K warm light against the labs' 5000 K — thirty meters underground, color temperature is time. The tree produces under 2% of one person-day of oxygen and keeps its floor area anyway; a design document should know which things do not belong in the numbers. The ECLSS loop has no exhaust port, only a feedstock port: concentrated CO₂ is piped to the surface Sabatier plant, so every exhaled breath ends up as rocket propellant.

And the pods. Residents sleep and eat here in World A, but work, gather and build in World B — the latest census says 51% now mainly live in B, 49% in A. On each pod's cradle rests the "headset" (by World B's own rules, possibly a decoy). The most common argument at dinner, three meters from a real tree under thirty meters of real rock: which side is real?

04

The clinic

One door off the main street: an imaging suite whose centerpiece is a faithful replica of a clinical whole-body PET/CT — ported, dimension by dimension, from its own design project.

The scanner follows the sibling PET/CT engineering study: Ø700 mm bore, 16-row CT up front, a static PET ring of 592 crystals × 64 rings in 37 modules behind it, and a two-stage table that reaches through both — whole-body protocol ~24 minutes. The replica keeps the design language too: gloss-white gantry, the cyan flare ring, orange PET modules visible down the bore, gold slip rings aft.

Around it, the room is built the way radiology actually works: a lead-partition control booth with a leaded-glass window and a three-screen console; an FDG pass-through hatch in the hot-lab wall with an amber dose window; crash cart, IV stand, wall-mounted reading display. Print-regolith skirting ties the white room back to the city that carved it.

06

What broke

The honest part.

  1. 13,902 triangles, zero pixels. The headless review pane reports innerWidth = 0; the camera aspect went NaN, the projection matrix was poisoned, and the renderer happily submitted the full scene to a screen that showed only sky. The hunt crawled through shader-compile checks and geometry NaN sweeps before landing on the actual fix: one || 1100 fallback on the canvas size.
  2. The hovering mushroom. The berm's brow lobe was top-clamped into a flat cap; from the air it read as a round table floating over the portal. Rebuilt twice — shrunk, lowered, and re-cut as a terrace below the main plateau before it read as landform.
  3. Everything floated 20 cm. The sandbox contract said "keep every vertex above y = 0.2 for terrain sinking"; the city convention wants assets flush at y = 0. All four undercity assets shipped hovering until a ground-normalization pass went into every build() — the validator now pins minY = 0.00.
  4. The 8 m pad that measured 9.6. A cable tray poked 1.6 m past the elevator station's pad, and declared size_m = 8 slid past the validator's 25% tolerance. Caught on re-read, tray trimmed onto the pad: bounding box now 8.0 exact.
  5. Cameras in the dark. Two interior review cams were placed outside the building's front wall — at night they returned pitch black, and one control-booth cam sat so close to its own screens the whole frame was blue glow. Interior cameras go inside; obvious only afterwards.
